changes.old: # Аугментация данных — Mixup, CutMix и политики преобразований A photograph of a cat can be cropped or reflected without necessarily changing the answer “cat.” A left-turn arrow cannot be reflected while keeping the answer “left.” Data augmentation constructs training examples by transforming existing ones. Choosing a transformation includes deciding what should happen to the target. Some transformations keep a class label, some transform an annotation along with the input, and some construct a mixture of targets. Mixup and CutMix belong to the last group. They do not require a pasted or blended image to have the unchanged label of its first parent. The examples use small tensors so that coordinates, target weights, losses, and gradients can be inspected. They do not measure recognition quality. The image galleries and comparison below are the authors' original figures, not new augmentation results generated for this book. ## Transform the input and its target together For classification, a label-preserving transformation asks for $f(T(x))$ to predict the same class as $f(x)$. In object detection, the target contains coordinates. Reflecting an image must also reflect its boxes. For segmentation, the class mask must undergo the same spatial transformation. Image and annotation cannot draw their geometric random choices independently.
changes.new: # Аугментация данных — Mixup, CutMix и политики преобразований Flip a photograph of a cat and the class is still “cat.” Flip a left-turn arrow and the class changes to “right.” When the target includes a box, its coordinates must follow the object even if the class stays the same. Mixup and CutMix start from two labelled images. Mixup blends their pixels; CutMix copies a patch from one image onto the other. Both change the class target as well as the input, but they determine the target weights differently. ## Transform the input and its target together In classification, a label-preserving transformation turns $(x,y)$ into $(T(x),y)$. The classifier is trained against the original label $y$ for both inputs. In object detection, the target contains coordinates. Reflecting an image must also reflect its boxes. For segmentation, the class mask must undergo the same spatial transformation. Image and annotation cannot draw their geometric random choices independently.

must become integers, and part of a centred rectangle may fall outside the image.
The nominal coefficient can therefore differ from the target weight.

Take two $4\times4$ images: A has class 0, B has class 1. At $\lambda=0.5$,
Mixup averages every pair of corresponding pixels and gives target
$(0.5,0.5)$. For CutMix, start with the same nominal $\lambda$ and a
$2\times2$ rectangle. In the middle of the image, four of sixteen pixels
come from B, giving target $(0.75,0.25)$. At a corner only one pixel is
pasted after clipping, giving target $(15/16,1/16)$.

Suppose the classifier assigns the corner example probabilities $(0.8,0.2)$.
The cross-entropy gradient on the class-0 logit is $0.8-15/16=-0.1375$.
Using the nominal target $(0.5,0.5)$ gives $0.8-0.5=+0.3$ instead.
With the correct target the loss favours a larger class-0 logit; with the
nominal target it favours a smaller one.
